thread.title: Don't Think Too Hard: Buy Visa - Visa Inc. (NYSE:V)

author: Detroit Bear
title: Don't Think Too Hard: Buy Visa - Visa Inc. (NYSE:V)
text:
Shares of Visa ( V ) sold off after some semi-negative commentary on Q2 revenue growth during its Q1’19 earnings call last week. However, shares rebounded quickly, eating into some of the upside potential. Still, based on a solid view for the rest of the year, aggressive share repurchases and robust secular growth trends, I believe shares are worth around $155. Let’s take a look at Q1 results, and why investors can expect to earn outsized returns with the payments provider.
Q1 – Top Line Growth Robust As Volume Chugs Along The most powerful tailwind of the Visa business model is the overwhelming move from cash to non-cash payments, be it credit card, Apple Pay ( AAPL ) or another digital wallet. Visa, given its size and the ability to grow its issuer network, continues to be the biggest beneficiary, with revenue growth up 13% y/y to $5.5 billion driven largely by a 11% constant currency growth in processed payment volume, as well as an 11% growth rate in total transactions processed. Debit slightly outpaced credit, up 13% ex-currency versus 9% growth in credit payments. Visa’s Data Processing revenue, which is earned for authorization, clearing, settlement, and network access, is outpacing the rest of the company, with revenue 15% y/y to $2.5 billion. Some of this is attributable to Visa’s value-add services like improved security through tokenization, which is allowing the company to improve price on some transactions.
Visa also continues to drive innovation in the physical card transaction, with tap to pay about to come to the United States in a major way as key partner Chase ( JPM ) starts to roll out the technology. Outside of the US, tap to pay accounts for 44% of domestic face-to-face transactions. This is an increase of 800 basis points compared to Q1’18, and I believe the technology continues to possess fantastic long-term potential to mitigate some shift to mediums like Apple Pay. Interestingly, the technology had a failure in the US earlier in the decade, but I believed increased POS adoption would make it a success this time around.
